attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, given as his own analysis.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the sentence scope, the parsing-system exception and the claim that no reliable method was known. It is asserted without hedging. Being listed among his 'guesses' only hedges whether it caused Amazon's choice.

contract.note: Limiting the claim to natural-language output and reading 'reliably' as dependable across ordinary requests is fair. But the universal 'nobody knows' needs broad evaluations that isolate the interpretation step, and none are in the packet.

evidence.note: The Sept 2022 Code as Policies preprint shows LLMs writing robot code from commands. That is code generation, which the contract excludes. It gives no reliability measure for interpreting sentences.

The researchers' own Nov 2022 blog (a company disclosure) admits they cannot tell in advance whether generated code will work, and that complex instructions are hard. This is partial support only; it covers one method.
SayCan reports 84% planning and 74% execution success on 101 tasks. That is substantial but imperfect. The aggregate results do not isolate language interpretation.

reviews.rationale: In 2022 there were working routes from language to action (CaP, SayCan), each with acknowledged limits and real failure rates. No source isolates how reliably sentences were turned into actions, or surveys the methods broadly enough to settle 'nobody knows'. The packet's own gaps say so.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The antecedent is kept. 'Best guesses' and 'I suspect' hedge whether the item explains Amazon's choice, not the conditional itself, which is stated with a firm 'would'.

contract.note: Reading 'mostly unmeetable' as most expected capabilities being unmet, and requiring expectation research before and after adoption, is an ordinary reading. The result depends on that evaluator-chosen measure.

evidence.note: Amazon's disclosure (updated July 2026) describes broad, natural conversation in Alexa+. It goes only to the antecedent, as a company claim, and says nothing about user expectations.
A single Consumer Reports reviewer found Alexa+ far more capable and used it more. One household cannot show changes in expectations across the population, or what share was met.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent plausibly occurred with Alexa+. But the packet has no representative study of user expectations before and after conversational Alexa, or of what share of them were met, so the early-resolution rule is not met. No deadline was stated.

attribution.note: Marcus's own 'bottom line' statement in his post.

semantics.note: The firm present-tense part is kept. The hedged 'may never be' is rightly left out and not scored.

contract.note: Testing dependable recovery of intended meaning in 2022 evaluations, not narrow intent classification, is an ordinary reading of 'not great tech for reliably inferring user intent'.

evidence.note: Ruis et al. (Oct 2022) found most models near random on simple implicature, and even intent-aligned models well short of humans. This meets the support condition.
InstructGPT (Mar 2022) shows relative gains in following instructions. Gains alone do not show dependable recovery of intended meaning.

reviews.rationale: A contemporary primary evaluation found systematic failure to recover implied meaning in GPT-3-class models, including instruction-tuned ones, which still fell well short of humans. InstructGPT's improvements do not show consistently dependable understanding. 'Not great' is supported for 2022.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: A firm forecast that the milestone is distant, with no deadline. Scope (home control, conversation, reliability, millions of homes) is kept.

contract.note: Setting 'millions' at two million or more homes and 'reliable' at dependable, not perfect, is ordinary. Declining to invent a calendar deadline is fair. Whether arrival around 2025–26 is 'long, long way' depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Amazon (Sept 2026) says tens of millions joined Early Access and Alexa+ runs on LLMs. That counts customers, not homes reliably using home control, and it is a company claim.
One Consumer Reports reviewer (Dec 2025) found natural-language home control working well, with bugs. There is no reliability measure at household scale.

reviews.rationale: Alexa+ shows an LLM-based conversational home-control product deployed widely about 2–3 years after the post. But the packet has no representative reliability data tied to millions of homes, and customer counts are not homes. The early-resolution rule is not met, and no deadline was given.
